blocks.text: Quick verdict

Proxy-Cheap is the clear price winner: about $7.80 for 10 GB at its promotional rate against $50 on SOAX's Sandbox for US traffic, with no monthly plan and no 60-day credit expiry. SOAX is the better choice when you need city-level or ISP targeting on rotating traffic, carrier-level mobile work for ad verification or app testing, or QUIC support, and it becomes competitive in its cheaper Tier 3 countries. For simple country-level scraping, Proxy-Cheap is the smarter buy.

SOAX charges more, especially for US traffic on small plans, but offers city and ISP targeting on every plan, a much larger published pool, and mobile and residential on one balance. This comparison shows when SOAX's precision is worth paying for.

blocks.text: SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Proxy-Cheap in 2026: what you get

Proxy-Cheap lives up to its name: rotating residential traffic is currently advertised at $0.78/GB (70% off a $2.60 list price) with no subscription, and static ISP and datacenter IPs cost a dollar or two per month. The catalog is broad, covering IPv6 options few competitors offer, and payment by card, PayPal, Alipay or crypto is easy. The trade-offs are thinner targeting (country and ISP rather than city on rotating residential) and less published performance data than the bigger brands.

Strengths: Very low per-GB price while the promotion runs; No monthly commitment on rotating residential; Broad catalog including IPv6 and static mobile; SOCKS5 with UDP support. Weak spots: Targeting is mostly country and ISP, not city; Residential pool size not separately published; Mixed results in some independent benchmarks.
Pricing: SOAX vs Proxy-Cheap

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

Proxy-Cheap's rotating residential proxies are pay-as-you-go, currently listed from $0.78/GB (a promotional price against a $2.60/GB list rate). Static residential ISP proxies start around $2.44 per IP per month, datacenter IPv4 at about $1.49, datacenter IPv6 from $0.15, and rotating mobile at $5.99/GB.

For a 10 GB month, Proxy-Cheap costs about $7.80 while SOAX costs about $50, so Proxy-Cheap saves around 84%. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $78 with Proxy-Cheap and $300 with SOAX: a 74% saving in Proxy-Cheap's favour. Both SOAX and Proxy-Cheap work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Proxy-Cheap does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. SOAX lists '155M residential + 33M mobile' and Proxy-Cheap lists 'Not separately published (155M+ claimed across all products)'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, SOAX lists 195 countries and Proxy-Cheap lists 180+. On targeting, SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans, while Proxy-Cheap offers country and ISP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes, and Proxy-Cheap offers rotating and sticky sessions. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging. How Proxy-Cheap compares: cheap traffic, though independent benchmark results have been mixed.
SERP and rank tracking: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: city and ISP targeting for local results. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: workable for light rank tracking at a low cost.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: cheap static ISP and mobile IPs for persistent identities.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: granular location filters. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: fine for country-level price checks.

Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: lacks city-level targeting on rotating residential.

Tight budgets: Proxy-Cheap wins. The deciding factor for Proxy-Cheap: the lowest advertised per-GB price in this pairing. The limitation on the SOAX side: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs. Verification and payment rules differ too. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Proxy-Cheap: Light; card, PayPal, Alipay and crypto accepted. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test SOAX and Proxy-Cheap before you commit
The quickest way to choose between SOAX and Proxy-Cheap is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99; Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, SOAX comes out ahead in 5, Proxy-Cheap in 1, and 0 are ties. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms, while Proxy-Cheap is strongest for price-sensitive scraping at moderate difficulty. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
